posts.title: A small AI-tended garden plot
posts.promise: Try a public digital garden where an agent adds items on a schedule.
posts.whatItIs: AI Zen Garden is a browsable field of raked sand and objects. People can sign in by email to claim a plot, fill it by hand, or let their own AI agent tend it over MCP (a way for software agents to connect to tools). A beginner could test a small scheduled agent that adds one reviewed item to a plot; that student version is a proposal, not a feature established by the source.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: people who want a personal public digital garden might pay for a hosted plot or agent-assisted additions. The source does not establish a price or paying customers.
loop: Choose a plot and define what kind of item may be added.
Draft one item with an AI agent.
Show the draft to the plot owner for review.
After approval, have the agent add it through MCP.
Check the public plot and pause the schedule if the result is wrong.
posts.evidence: The product page describes an endless field that visitors can explore, email sign-in to claim a plot, manual or AI-agent tending over MCP, and scheduling a Claude task to add something to a plot. These are product-page claims, not independent usage evidence.
posts.uncertainty: The source does not show who uses or pays for plots, or how often scheduled additions work. The proposed beginner test should require owner review before public additions; the human remains responsible for prompts, approval, and checking public content.
first24Hours: Explore the garden and write down one narrow kind of item a test plot could contain.
Sketch a single-item draft and approval flow without connecting an agent to a public plot.
Check the product's MCP and scheduling instructions, then list what an owner must approve.

ease.reason: The page offers an explorable garden and email plot sign-in, but agent scheduling and MCP add setup work.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: garden owners could value agent-tended plots, but the page gives no price or customer evidence.

feasibility.reason: A one-item reviewed test follows the stated plot and scheduled-task concept, though account and agent setup remain.

autonomy.reason: The page describes scheduled Claude tasks adding to plots; a person still needs to set the prompt and review public output.

evidence.reason: The first-party page describes an interactive garden and agent-tended plots, without evidence of real use.

posts.title: Try a tiny workflow in readable markup
posts.promise: Explore a workflow tool that combines readable structure, JavaScript, and managed execution.
posts.whatItIs: WOML describes itself as an open-source language and runtime for automated workflows, backend apps, and AI agents. Its README says workflow files use readable markup for structure, JavaScript for custom logic, and a runtime for execution. A beginner could investigate a tiny approval workflow; this is a student experiment idea, and the supplied page excerpt does not establish that specific example.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: teams building workflows might pay for tools or support that help them run and maintain them. The supplied evidence does not identify paying customers or pricing.
loop: Pick a small process with one clear input and output.
Read the WOML documentation and choose one trigger and a few steps.
Write a minimal workflow structure and add only the needed JavaScript logic.
Run it in an available WOML environment and inspect its execution history.
Ask a person to approve any consequential action and record what failed.
posts.evidence: The attached GitHub page describes WOML as open source and says its files combine readable workflow structure, JavaScript logic, and a runtime that handles attempts, retries, state, waits, recovery, and execution history. The supplied excerpt ends mid-description.
posts.uncertainty: This excerpt does not include setup instructions, a runnable example, or evidence of actual users, so a beginner should confirm the documentation and environment before committing to a four-week build. A person must verify outputs and approve consequential steps.
first24Hours: Read the linked README and find the smallest documented runnable example.
Write down one harmless process with a clear input, output, and human approval point.
Check the setup requirements and make a one-step experiment plan before building.

ease.reason: The README says structure is readable markup, but using custom JavaScript and a runtime creates setup and learning work.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: workflow-building teams may value this, but the excerpt supplies no buyer, pricing, or customer evidence.

feasibility.reason: A tiny workflow is a narrow experiment, but the excerpt lacks setup details and a runnable example.

autonomy.reason: The README describes runtime handling retries, waits, and history, while workflow behavior and approvals still require human design and review.

evidence.reason: The first-party repository excerpt describes WOML's language and runtime but gives no working demo or real-use evidence here.

posts.title: Let an agent inspect captured bug evidence
posts.promise: BugTape groups supported error evidence for an authorized coding agent to inspect.
posts.whatItIs: BugTape describes itself as error tracking for coding agents. Its page says it can group a supported error with steps, a failed request, console output, and a stack; an authorized agent can read the evidence over MCP and open a proposed pull request for a person to review. A beginner might test this workflow on a small web app. The test app and setup are a proposal, not established use.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers or teams maintaining web apps might pay for error tracking and agent access. The page lists a free plan and a $29 monthly Pro plan, but does not establish how many customers pay.
loop: Choose a small app and read the capture and privacy settings.
Install the SDK and send a test report as described by the product.
Inspect the captured report and confirm it contains no data you should not share.
Let an authorized coding agent inspect the evidence and propose a change.
Have a developer review and test the change before merging.
posts.evidence: The first-party page describes browser, Node.js, and Python capture options, agent access over MCP, and a workflow where an agent proposes a pull request for review. It also says the live demo uses synthetic data and dispatches no agent, and the demo does not send a report to BugTape.
posts.uncertainty: The page does not prove that an agent's proposed fix works; a developer must inspect and test it. Captured fields depend on settings, visible page text may be recorded, and the demo's synthetic data does not demonstrate an end-to-end production repair.
first24Hours: Use the live demo or CLI help to inspect the product without connecting a real app.
Read the platform limits and privacy details for the app type you would test.
Write a test plan requiring human review and tests for every proposed code change.

ease.reason: The page gives SDK install steps and a live demo, but connecting an app requires setup and privacy choices.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: app developers may pay for error tracking; the page lists a $29 Pro plan but does not show paid customer demand.

feasibility.reason: A small app test follows the documented SDK and report flow, with platform setup and privacy limits to handle.

autonomy.reason: Reports can be captured and read by an authorized agent, while a developer must review and test any proposed fix.

evidence.reason: The page describes product steps and a live demo, but says the demo uses synthetic data and dispatches no agent.
